name: Femi Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the sauté section at a brasserie in the old market district, so pans, sauces and fish, about 200 covers on a busy night. I'm in at eleven to do prep and out around eleven at night. I use an AI app on my phone every day, mostly to write my prep list and work out costs when I'm trying a new special.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the specials board, because Anya, the head chef, lets me put one dish on it each week. What wears me out is the heat, and the dishwasher breaking down every second Saturday. I also run a supper club with a friend once a month, which is my real love, though it barely breaks even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so: it's a tool, not a chef. Honestly, I'd post that with a photo of my prep list. People at the brasserie already tease me for talking to my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I like the tools, and I'd hoped they'd get good fast enough to help me run my own place one day. But for my job and my wages, nothing really moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the apps for costing and the prep list, and push the supper club to twice a month. I'd save toward a deposit on a small food unit, maybe five years out. And I'd keep asking Anya to teach me the ordering side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the supper club bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good night, after food and the hall hire, maybe 200 between the two of us. It's not real money yet, it's practice at running something. The supper club is where I learn to be a boss, and the brasserie is where I learn to be a cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the deposit come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, from my wages and the supper club. I've got about four months of bills saved now, and I'd want to keep that untouched. The deposit pot would sit on top of it.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool, not a chef**, and post my prep list to prove it.
I'd laugh along with colleagues who already tease me for **talking to my phone**.
think: Privately I'd be a little **disappointed**, because I hoped better tools would help me open a place.
For my own **job and wages**, nothing really moves in this picture.
do: Run the **supper club** twice a month instead of once.
Save towards a **deposit** on a small food unit about five years out.
Keep asking the head chef to teach me **ordering**.
feel: **Calm** and slightly flat, like a promise that didn't arrive.
S0.quote: The supper club is where I learn to be a boss, and the brasserie is where I learn to be a cook.
fieldNote: He is the rare cook who is **let down** that AI stays small.
His **four months** of savings is a line he won't cross, even for his dream.
The **supper club** is his training ground for owning a business, not a money-maker yet.

steps.text: Keep learning the brasserie's ordering side from the head chef
Run the supper club twice a month instead of once
Save towards a deposit on a small food unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be a cook who's good with tech. Kitchens still need hands, and the boring paperwork gets lighter. I'd probably say that loudly, too loudly maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it helps me more than most. Ordering, costing, the allergy sheets and the rota are the work that keeps cooks from becoming sous chefs, and I can already do it with the apps. The risk is robots on the fryer and prep side, but they'd come slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Anya and offer to take over the ordering and costing with the new software, for a bit more money. I'd learn whatever system the owners pick in the first week it arrives. And I'd use AI to plan the supper club menus and shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about saying so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the lads on prep and the dishwasher are the ones robots reach first, even slowly. Kofi on prep has been there eight years. The same software that makes me a sous chef could make Kofi, our prep cook of eight years, a spare pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything for Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him the ordering app, if he wanted. He mostly doesn't want to. I can't make that choice for him.

say: I'd say it's a **good time** to be a cook who's good with tech.
I'd tell people kitchens still **need hands** while the paperwork gets lighter.
think: Privately I'd see **ordering and costing** as the ladder to sous chef, and I already use the apps.
The real risk is robots on **prep and frying**, which would come slowly.
do: Offer to run **ordering and costing** on the new software for more pay.
Learn whatever system the owners pick in its **first week**.
Plan **supper club** menus and shopping lists with AI.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt about feeling that way.
S1.quote: The same software that makes me a sous chef could make Kofi, our prep cook of eight years, a spare pair of hands.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion route**, because the thinking tasks are his edge.
His **guilt** about the long-serving prep cook is real, but he won't push help on him.
He'd move in the **first week**, well ahead of most of the kitchen.

steps.text: Offer to run ordering and costing on the new software for more pay
Grow the supper club using AI to plan menus and shopping

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to build something people want from a human. Something upbeat like that, because I'd mean part of it. At work I'd say learn everything you can now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's tight. The thinking side of my job, the costing and ordering I was going to use to get ahead, goes to AGI in 2028, so that ladder disappears. Then around 2031 robots come for the cooking, and I'd be 32 with maybe a food unit I've just borrowed for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd drop the five-year plan and try to turn the supper club into a weekend pop-up within a year, selling the idea that a real person cooks your food. I'd keep the brasserie job for the wage until the robots actually arrive. I'd also apply to the robot kitchen companies, because someone has to set the machines up and fix them, and I'd rather be that person than be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Half thrilled, half scared I'm wrong about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people pay more for food a human cooked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, the way people pay for handmade bread. Not everyone, and not every night. I'm betting my savings that people will pay extra to watch a real person burn their fingers on a pan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you risk if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four months of savings, and my mum's patience. She already thinks the supper club is a hobby. If it flops, I go back to a line somewhere, while there are still lines.

say: I'd say now is the moment to build **something human-made** people want.
At work I'd tell everyone to **learn everything** they can while there's time.
think: Privately, AGI in 2028 takes away the **costing and ordering** ladder I was counting on.
By 2031 robots reach the cooking, and I'd be **32** with a fresh business loan.
do: Put savings into turning the supper club into a **weekend pop-up** within a year.
Keep the **brasserie wage** until robots actually arrive.
Apply to **kitchen robot firms** to install and fix their machines.
feel: **Wired**: half thrilled, half scared he's wrong about everything.
S2.quote: I'm betting my savings that people will pay extra to watch a real person burn their fingers on a pan.
fieldNote: The fast picture **removes his edge**, since the thinking tasks he mastered are automated first.
He bets on people paying a **premium** for food a real person cooks.
He'd hedge by working **for the robot makers**, not just against them.

steps.text: Put savings into turning the supper club into a weekend pop-up
Keep the brasserie job for the wage until robots arrive
Apply to kitchen robot firms to install and fix their machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. I'd tell the younger cooks to pick up something next to cooking now. That's what I'd say at the pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, five years gives me a proper run. I'd be 32 when AGI arrives and 35 when the robots get to kitchens, so I could build the pop-up into something real and maybe learn to service the machines on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years, I'd grow the supper club into a weekend pop-up and register it as a business. I'd take a short course in kitchen equipment repair, because a robot fryer is still a fryer. Once AGI arrived, I'd use it for everything on the business side, from the books to the bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit restless, like I'm already late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Equipment repair is a big step from sauté. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every kitchen I've worked in has had a combi oven, the big steam oven, break down on a Friday. The repair guy charges a fortune and everyone's grateful anyway. Whoever can fix the robot fryer at nine on a Friday night will have work long after the cooks are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at home change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay in the shared flat longer than I want to. My flatmates are fine with it. A cheap room is what pays for the pop-up.

say: I'd say **five years** is a gift if you use it.
I'd tell younger cooks to learn a **second skill** next to cooking now.
think: Privately I'd have until **35** before kitchen robots, which is a proper run.
That's enough time to build the pop-up and learn to **service machines**.
do: Register the supper club as a **weekend pop-up** business within two years.
Take a short course in **equipment repair**.
Run the pop-up's books and bookings with **AI** after 2031.
feel: **Hopeful** but restless, as if already late.
S3.quote: Whoever can fix the robot fryer at nine on a Friday night will have work long after the cooks are gone.
fieldNote: His repair idea comes from watching **broken ovens** stop service on busy Fridays.
He'll stay in a **shared flat** to fund the business, a trade-off he accepts easily.
Five years turns his plan from a gamble into a **sequence**.

steps.text: Register the supper club as a weekend pop-up business
Take a short course in kitchen equipment repair
Run the pop-up's books and bookings with AI after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years. Anyone in hospitality could plan for that. I'd say it kindly, though, because not everyone has my head for this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives and 40 when robots get to kitchens around 2039, and by then I'd want to own a small place, not work a line. The extra three years for hands-on work matters less to me than having time to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the original plan but faster: deposit saved in three years, small restaurant open in five. I'd put AI into the business side from day one. I'd also try a few robot tools as they come out, like a dishwashing robot or a robot fryer, so I know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Calm, with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it a contradiction for a human-cooking restaurant to use robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. I'd want robots on the dishes and the fryer, and me on the food people see. I'd happily let a robot wash my pans if it means I can afford to stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say get a proper job. Then she'd come to opening night and tell everyone her son owns a restaurant.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** for anyone with ten years' warning.
I'd say it kindly, since not everyone is **comfortable with tech**.
think: Privately, ten years suits me, because by **40** I want to own a place, not work a line.
The **extra three years** for hands-on work matters less than time to build.
do: Save a **deposit** for a small unit within three years.
Open a **small restaurant** within five years, with AI on the business side.
Trial **robot tools** like a dishwasher or fryer as they appear.
feel: **Calm**, with a clear list of what comes next.
S4.quote: I'd happily let a robot wash my pans if it means I can afford to stay open.
fieldNote: With a decade he is **confident**, and frames it as a matter of planning.
He's comfortable using **robots backstage** while selling human cooking out front.
His mother's doubt is a **gentle pressure** he jokes about rather than resents.

steps.text: Save a deposit for a small restaurant unit within three years
Open a small restaurant within five years
Trial a dishwashing robot and a robot fryer as they appear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes away my ladder and the robots arrive before my place is paid off. What would help is cheap small-business loans and short, practical courses, like a few weekends on equipment repair, not a three-year degree.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd cook. Every picture you read me ends with machines, but nobody's built a machine that knows when a sauce needs another minute.

headlineQuote: Every picture you read me ends with machines, but nobody's built a machine that knows when a sauce needs another minute.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old sauté cook** at a busy brasserie who uses AI apps every day.
He runs a monthly **supper club** with a friend and dreams of owning a small restaurant.
He sees Steady Disruption as a **ladder**, since he already handles costing and ordering with software.
**AGI by 2028** worries him because that ladder disappears and robots arrive before his plans pay off.
With five or ten years, he would build a business and learn **equipment repair**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which removes his route up and brings robots before his restaurant pays off.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small-business loans** and short practical courses, like weekend repair training.
